speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF FARM CREDIT ACT IN EASTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Lapointe asked me the following question:
Can the minister inquire and report to this house why there are so many delays and refusals in the implementation of the Farm Credit Act in eastern Canada, and especially in the districts of Lake St. John, Saguenay and in my constituency of Lapointe?
I am informed by the Farm Credit Corporation that the percentage of loan refusals in eastern Canada is not significantly different from that in the rest of Canada, and that in Quebec in particular the percentage of refusals has been less than the national average.
Inquiries of the Ministry
There has been some delay, however, in the processing of applications in Quebec due to the unprecedented increase in the number of applications received. In 1961 by the end of June the corporation had received only 40 applications for loans. In 1962 by June 30, 291 applications had been received. By the same date this year 929 farmers had applied for loans, or about 23 times as many applications as were received two years earlier.
Since the spring of 1962 the corporation has increased its field staff in Quebec from 4 to 26 men. It takes time to recruit and train the men to do this kind of work, but the situation is well in hand and the work will be up to date by the end of the current appraisal season. Because of the large volume of applications received in the constituencies to which the hon. member for Lapointe referred, the corporation has assigned 4 men to bring the work up to date in this area.
Applications received expressed as a percentage of farmers interviewed are 50 per cent for all Canada and 59 per cent in Quebec. The percentage of applications rejected or withdrawn after appraisal of farm is 8.5 per cent for all Canada and 6 per cent for Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, before that happens may I address a point to the government in regard to this question; it will possibly affect their thinking in regard to this particular point. The discussion last night was germane to those contracts which did not have a pecuniary penalty and where a building was actually being built for an owner. I would submit to the Minister of Finance- I think he has received representations in this regard-that in the commercial field and in the industrial field particularly buildings are often erected for purposes of very long term lease, where contracts have actually been signed to lease the building at a stated rent based upon the amortization of the cost of the building.
Clause 9 as proposed does not take into account any contract of this type. Certainly with regard to the province of Ontario I would suggest that a very important segment of the commercial and industrial construction field or realty field will be adversely affected. I think these people would be caught in the provision by that passage wherein it is said that property in the goods must pass. I say this because we know that under a lease property in the goods does not pass; the contractor retains ownership in the goods while the building is leased. I would put it to the minister that if it is still part of the philosophy of the budget to stimulate industry and maintain economic progress, this is one sector to which much closer attention should be paid and in regard to which appropriate modifications should be considered favourably by

the government. I should like to ask the minister to comment upon that point.

speechtext: I can assure the hon. member that this matter has been under careful consideration. We came to the conclusion in our consideration that with the staging of the application of the tax and with the extension of the period of exemption to the end of 1964, that was as far as we could go without opening the thing wider.
In other words, there will be no tax exemption whatsoever with respect to buildings erected for leasing purposes?

(ii) after June 13, 1963, if the contract was entered into

Mr. Chairman, I naturally appreciate the minister's presenting an amendment which substantially responds to the amendment I proposed last night, except that the amendment in its original form would have eliminated certain ambiguities. I am a little concerned as to the way in which the officials of the department will interpret the clauses. I should like to ask the minister with regard to subparagraph (B), which contains the words "undertook expressly"-which are plain enough-and "or by necessary implication", who will decide whether or not there was such a necessary implication to hold the offer open till the specified period? Mr. Chairman, if I might answer that I think two things must be remarked upon. First of all, in any legal text dealing with taxation, such as customs or excise, an officer of the department, under the direction of the minister, always has to an extent to interpret or to apply the text; as a matter of fact, by applying it he is also interpreting it. When he is in doubt about it, or the validity of his interpretation is placed in doubt by the taxpayer, there will then of necessity be a reference to the Department of Justice. The normal consequence is that if there is then no understanding it becomes a matter which only the courts can settle.
The question here is whether the text is satisfactory to the hon. member, who as we know is a good lawyer. Is the text sufficient in his opinion exactly to convey the legal consequences or the protection which he has in mind? I think it is. Whether it be this text or another text, very often taxpayers will not agree with departmental officers, and if a ruling from the Department of Justice is not acceptable, then the matter has to resolve itself into a legal case. We hope to eliminate that as far as possible, but some are unavoidable. I am sure the hon. member will agree with me that there is no room here to define "undertook expressly or by necessary implication", which in French would be, of course, "expressement ou tacitement". I submit that we should not go further than that.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think that it is up to me to say what that plan will be. As a matter of fact, it will be one of the duties of the council, as stated in paragraph (a):
to assess the medium and long term prospects,
-and then to appraise the potentialities of growth in our Canadian economy.
In short, it is simply a question of attempting in Canada an experiment made in several European countries, without perhaps going as far as in France, but rather following the

example set by countries like the Netherlands and others where experts, in co-operation with industry, with the private sector, assess the potentialities of expansion, considering their resources and also the exigencies of a full employment policy.
After studying these possibilities, the council must then evaluate what could be the rate of growth of the economy as a whole in order to reach that objective. Then, discussions must be held with the governments and the private sector of the economy to find out what their plans are, if, at the start, the rate of growth were to be 4, 5 or 6 per cent, according to the initial suggestion.
There is no question here of elaborating a plan without consulting any one and then imposing it by control or coercion; on the contrary, it is only a matter of indicating the objectives to the economy and to ensure that the private sector and the other governments know them in a general way and are doing their best to adapt to them freely.

The government in our society is expected, quite rightly, to take the lead in both formulating and ranking national objectives. Economic Council of Canada

I feel this exchange of ideas between the representatives of labour and management has taught both of these important groups in our country how to live with one another.
This is the crux of a great many of the problems that face this country. So long as labour and management can understand one another, so long as they can exchange their ideas, then many of the problems faced by the government and the economy of this country will be alleviated. I say that great strides, have been made in this area through the efforts of the national productivity council. I suggest to the minister that when he is considering appointments to this national economic council, consideration should be given to the selection of some of these people who have served so well on the national productivity council, because of their background of experience in this field. I believe their

speechtext:
Several members have expressed the fear that under this legislation the minister might go too fast in moving toward the establishment of a planned economy. I suggest that anyone who will read this bill carefully, particularly clause 9, will have his fears allayed. I do not believe there is any danger under this legislation of either going very fast or getting very close to a planned economy, not even indicative planning. If one reads through the clauses one sees in each case such phrases as, to recommend; to consider; to study means; to study economic growth; to explore and evaluate; to encourage maximum consultation; to seek regular consultation, and so on.
The powers given to this board are extremely limited. When the minister talks about economic planning in France and makes a comparison with this legislation, I think one has to stretch his imagination rather far to think there will be anything resembling the planning operation in France. However, it is a beginning, and as a beginning it ought to be encouraged. The value of this beginning will largely depend on the economic council itself and the personnel of that council.
I wanted to hear the minister answer the question which was asked by my colleague, the hon. member for Port Arthur. He wanted the minister to outline the distinction in functions between the chairman and the two full time directors on the one hand, and the number of members of the council who, of course, will be merely attending the meetings of council on a per diem basis. This group, perhaps up to 25 in number, will have what functions? How will the chairman and the two directors function? What will be their duties and what will be the duties of the other members? Are they to be largely advisory? Will they meet three or four times a year? It is suggested here that there will be representatives from appropriate organizations. Will they be nominated by those organizations? Will the minister ask each organization for a slate of candidates? Will the manufacturers' association, the Canadian Labour Congress, the farmers' union or co-operative, be asked to submit a slate of names from which the minister may choose? Will the government simply select a farmer and say he represents agriculture, although agriculture may have had no voice in suggesting his name? Will some ex-unionist or defeated candidate who once had trade union connections, be chosen as a representative of labour or will labour be able to nominate a man who
2876	HOUSE OF
Economic Council of Canada will be able to speak for labour and take the views of the council back to labour?
I am convinced that the success or failure of this economic council will depend upon the participation of the groups that are represented on the council. Unless you get the cooperation of industry, labour, agriculture and all the various segments of the economy, then the council is going to be little more than a statistics gathering organization putting together plans that will gather dust on somebody's desk. If the members of this council are representatives of organizations and are able to go back and secure the co-operation of these organizations, this could be a very effective council. I should like, therefore, to ask the minister, first, what is the distinction between the full time members and the part time members? Will the members who are selected from organizations be selected on the basis of the organizations having an opportunity to name a slate? Will all these persons concerned be expected to report back and secure the co-operation of the organizations they are alleged to represent?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND DEFINITION OF DUTIES
speechtext:
I am not raising any point of order, Mr. Chairman, but I think this probably comes well within this clause of the bill. I want to refer to the matter raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur as to the question of the inclusion of natural resources. Anyone looking at clause 9 can see that there has been a lot of care and attention given to it. It has been honed and sharpened, and its words carefully chosen; but as the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration will realize, there is a very important motto which we have to the effect that the inclusion of one is the exclusion of the other, and specifically mentioned from clause (a) to clause (k) are a number of specific definite duties without having reference to the question of natural resources. This rules out the fact that natural resources can be considered.
I doubt very much whether this statute will ever be the subject of judicial determination, but it is our duty to consider that the words of the statute give effect to the announced intention. If it is the announced intention of the government, in this question of planning, to deal with natural resources, then it simply has not done it. It is not good enough to say these sections are wide enough, taken one with the other, reading one in juxtaposition with another, to include something which is not specifically mentioned.
I suggest that after the words in paragraph (g) which state:
-to study how national economic policies can best foster the balanced economic development of all areas of Canada
-there should be added "and the development of the natural resources of Canada".
[Mr. Douglas.!

I come from an area where, because of the policies of national development of the last government, with the construction of the Pine Point railway and other matters, the area is now beginning to flex its industrial muscles, based on its natural resources, and I am concerned to see that in any planning which takes place there is careful and meticulous attention paid to this part of our national life.
I took some exception to what the hon. member for Kootenay West said about people from Alberta, and I should remind him that there are some great tourists who go from Alberta to B.C., not least of which is the premier of B.C. But apart from that I think his speech was on very sound ground.
I do not want to suggest that what is done in another country is the same thing as should be done in Canada, but I would refer to the language used in England when the United Kingdom introduced a similar operation, not by the introduction of a statute but by simple executive act. The definition of the tasks of the national economic development council of that country was given by the then chancellor Selwyn Lloyd within the four corners of three simple paragraphs:
To examine the economic performance of the nation with particular concern for plans for the future in both the private and the public sectors of industry;
to consider together what are the obstacles to quicker growth, what can be done to improve efficiency and whether the best use is being made of our resources, and
to seek agreement upon ways of improving the economic performance, competitive power and efficiency, in other words to increase the rate of sound growth.
That is excellently worded and I think could well have formed the basis of the objectives in clause 9.
I do not go so far as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam in talking about indicative and other types of plan. We have heard of carrying coals to Newcastle, but here is a case of coals from Newcastle.
There is a news item in The Christian Science Monitor of Monday, May 27, 1963 under the heading, "Soviet Banker Sounds Alarm". I did not know they had Soviet bankers, but apparently they can be as alarmed as our bankers, because in his opinion the type of planning they have in the Soviet union has gone too far and too fast. This is what the article says in part:
Delegation of powers, uneconomic prices, and rapid industrial growth without checks and balances have plunged tens of thousands of Soviet enterprises into relative or absolute bankruptcy.
In the Economic Gazette of May 11, Aleksandr K. Korovushkin, Soviet state bank president, has sounded alarm. In the first four months of this year, 11 large enterprises have informed the bank that they had to stop payments.

The whole Soviet financial planning system seems to be out of gear. While production continues at full blast-mueh of it unplanned and unneeded- more and more Industries are going into the red.
I am satisfied that something along the lines of what was done in the United Kingdom is fine. I believe that while there has been too much prolixity in clause 9 it is probably along those lines, but I would like to see some specific mention of the words "natural resources".
